meta.competitionFrequencyPerWeek: 1–2 races per week at peak season; single-race duration ~1.5–14 min
meta.trainingFrequencyPerWeek: 6–9 track/road sessions (aerobic, threshold, interval, speed) + 2–3 gym
meta.notes: Middle distance (800 m–5 km) bridges the anaerobic intensity of sprinting and the aerobic demands of distance running. The 800 m is close to anaerobic in its lactate demands; the 5 km is predominantly aerobic with a critical-speed component. The gym plays a supporting but essential role: heavy, low-rep strength training improves running economy and aerobic endurance performance without adding non-propulsive mass. Reactive plyometrics (pogos, bounding) build tendon stiffness for a stiffer, more economical ground contact. Hamstring eccentric strength, calf/Achilles prehab, and tibial bone-stress management are the primary injury-prevention levers. Olympic lifting is optional; single-leg strength emphasis is high.

maxStrength.why: Heavy strength training (trap-bar DL, squat) improves running economy by enhancing neuromuscular efficiency and force per stride; a moderate priority — enough to drive economy gains without adding non-propulsive mass.
maxStrength.source: Blagrove 2018 (strength training for middle/long distance, Sports Med); Rønnestad & Mujika 2014

relativeStrength.why: Strength per kilogram is the relevant metric — economy improvements only materialise if mass is controlled. High relative strength drives force per stride without the metabolic cost of extra body weight.

explosivePower.why: Rate of force development contributes to running economy via a stiffer, shorter ground contact. More important at 800 m (decisive sprint finish) than at 5 km; a moderate priority across the discipline.

reactiveStrength.why: Tendon stiffness and SSC efficiency directly reduce the metabolic cost of running — a stiffer Achilles/calf complex returns elastic energy per stride. Reactive strength training (pogos, bounding) is one of the highest-transfer gym inputs for middle-distance performance.

sprintSpeed.why: A decisive sprint finish is a feature of 800 m and 1500 m racing; the capacity to accelerate in the final lap or straight separates elite competitors. Less relevant at 5 km but never negligible.

acceleration.why: Useful for tactical acceleration mid-race and final-lap kicks; less globally important than in pure sprint events but relevant for 800 m tactical surges.

deceleration.why: Pace management in middle distance rarely involves large decelerations; minor relevance to recovery between laps but not a primary driver.

changeOfDirection.why: Track racing is near-straight-line; COD is irrelevant to competitive performance and a very low training priority.

aerobicEndurance.why: The dominant energy system for 1500 m–5 km and still critical for 800 m — VO2max, lactate threshold, and aerobic capacity underpin competitive performance at all middle-distance events. The primary physiological target.

anaerobicEndurance.why: Lactate tolerance is decisive at 800 m and significant at 1500 m — the ability to sustain speed above VO2max pace defines tactical and finishing ability across all middle-distance events.
anaerobicEndurance.source: Gastin 2001; Billat (interval training and lactate kinetics)

repeatSprintAbility.why: Heats + finals scheduling over 2–3 days requires some capacity to repeat quality efforts; more relevant at 800/1500 m championship meets than at 5 km.

mobility.why: Hip extension range, hip-flexor flexibility, and ankle dorsiflexion affect running mechanics and stride length. Reduced ankle dorsiflexion and hip extension increase Achilles and tibial bone-stress injury risk.
mobility.source: running-biomechanics and injury-risk literature; expert consensus

stability.why: Pelvis-lumbar stability and single-leg stance stability underpin efficient energy transfer per stride and reduce injury risk (hip drop, knee valgus, tibial loading) over the thousands of strides in a race or training session.

rotationalPower.why: Arm drive and minimal trunk counter-rotation contribute to running mechanics; a secondary quality — trained mainly through sprint drills and anti-rotation core work rather than dedicated rotational loading.

gripStrength.why: No implement; arm swing and hand position matter for mechanics but grip strength is not a performance limiter.

neckStrength.why: No collision; head position influences running mechanics at high speed but neck strength is not a middle-distance performance limiter.

balance.why: Single-leg stance phases and uneven terrain (cross-country, road) require balance; relevant for injury prevention and single-leg gym exercises that build hip/ankle robustness.

coordination.why: Running economy is partly a coordination quality — arm drive, hip cycle, ground-contact mechanics, and A-skip/B-skip drill competency all contribute to efficiency at race pace.

durability.why: Middle-distance training volumes (60–100+ miles/week at high level) impose cumulative load on bones, tendons, and muscles — connective-tissue durability (Achilles, tibiae, hamstrings) is a meaningful performance limiter and career-longevity factor.

energySystems.workToRestRatio: Race is a single continuous maximal effort; training intervals 1:1–1:3 for VO2max work; 1:4–1:6 for speed and lactate work
energySystems.matchDemands: Aerobically biased across all events, with a decisive lactate-tolerance component that is GREATEST at 800 m and declines toward 5 km. The 800 m approaches a 50/50 aerobic/anaerobic split at elite pace; the 1500 m is ~75–80% aerobic; the 5 km is ~90–95% aerobic. The figures above represent a weighted midpoint across 800 m–5 km. Glycolytic demand drives finishing-speed capacity and tactical surging in all events; ATP-PC contributes only to initial acceleration and kick. Running economy and critical speed (the maximal speed sustainable via aerobic pathways) are the primary performance determinants.
energySystems.heartRateProfile: Near-maximal HR sustained for the duration of the race at all middle-distance events; VO2max typically reached within 60–90 s of maximal-effort running and maintained.
energySystems.fatigueProfile: Lactate accumulation and hydrogen-ion buffering capacity limit performance at 800/1500 m; at 5 km, fatigue is a blend of glycogen depletion, peripheral fatigue, and cardiovascular ceiling. Both aerobic capacity (VO2max) and the fraction of VO2max that can be sustained (lactate threshold, critical speed) are key determinants.
energySystems.source: Gastin 2001 energy-system contribution during maximal exercise
energySystems.notes: Event-dependence is large — the engine should read the event archetype (positions) for a more precise energy split rather than treating the 75/20/5 midpoint as universal.

primaryPatterns: sustained aerobic pace — economy and fatigue resistance
finishing kick (maximal sprint in final 200–400 m)
movementProfile.jointLoading: Achilles/calf complex and tibiae undergo high repetitive compressive and tensile loading across thousands of strides per session. Hamstring eccentric loading during late swing phase increases at faster paces. Patellofemoral joint loaded with each stride under fatigue. Hip abductors / glute medius stabilise the pelvis across every ground contact.
movementProfile.groundContacts: ~800–1200 ground contacts per km of running; middle-distance athletes accumulate many thousands per week across training volume.
movementProfile.landingDemands: Moderate-stiffness landing at near-forefoot or midfoot at race pace; plyometric training (pogos, bounding) introduces brief very-stiff landings to develop Achilles tendon stiffness.
movementProfile.jumping: No competitive jumping. Plyometric training (pogo, bounding, A-skip) is integral to stiffness and economy development.
movementProfile.rotating: Arm counter-rotation and trunk anti-rotation; minimal overt rotation.
movementProfile.repeatedImpacts: High-volume, moderate-to-high-force repetitive ground impacts in every training session. Tibial bone and Achilles tendon are the primary cumulative-load targets. Hamstring under eccentric load at faster paces.
movementProfile.asymmetricLoading: Asymmetric stride patterns are common and can drive unilateral injury risk; bilateral strength and contact-time symmetry should be monitored.
dominantMuscleGroups: calves / Achilles (primary tendon stiffness and propulsion unit)
hamstrings (eccentric late-swing loading, especially at fast paces)
hip abductors / glute medius (pelvic stability per stride)
core (anti-extension, anti-rotation, pelvic control over thousands of strides)
commonDeficiencies: insufficient calf/Achilles load capacity relative to training volume
hamstring eccentric strength deficit at fast paces
weak hip abductors driving hip drop (Trendelenburg) and knee valgus
poor tibialis anterior and intrinsic foot strength predisposing tibial bone stress
inadequate running economy (high metabolic cost of a given pace)

common.name: Hamstring strain (acute — higher incidence at faster paces)
common.incidence: moderate — more prevalent at 800 m/1500 m pace than long distance; driven by faster stride velocities and interval/speed work
common.severity: moderate (grade I–II typical; grade II = 1–4 weeks out)
common.mechanism: Eccentric loading of the biceps femoris long head during late swing phase at fast running velocities and during sprint finishes; risk increases with fatigue, training load spikes, and speed-work volume.
highRiskTissues: biceps femoris long head (proximal musculotendinous junction)
common.rtpConsiderations: Restore full eccentric hamstring strength, particularly at long muscle length; progressive reintroduction of interval then race-pace running before maximal sprint work; Nordic curl protocol through RTP.
common.source: Askling hamstring-strain literature; van Dyk et al.; Petersen 2011 Nordic hamstring RCT

common.name: Achilles tendinopathy (chronic overuse)
common.incidence: high in middle-distance runners — the most common chronic soft-tissue injury across all running disciplines; driven by high repetitive Achilles loading
common.severity: moderate-high if unmanaged (often chronic; can sideline athletes for months)
common.mechanism: Cumulative compressive and tensile load on the Achilles tendon from high training volume, combined with insufficient tendon-load management, inadequate recovery, and training surface changes. Rapid increases in interval-training volume or pace are a common precipitant.
common.rtpConsiderations: Heavy slow resistance and isometric calf loading (Alfredson / Silbernagel protocol); graduated return to impact with symptom monitoring; address biomechanical and load-management drivers before full return.
common.source: Alfredson H, Silbernagel K — Achilles tendinopathy eccentric and heavy slow resistance loading literature

common.name: Patellofemoral pain (runner's knee)
common.incidence: moderate — common in female runners and during training volume build-phases; exacerbated by hill and downhill running
common.severity: low-moderate (often self-limiting if managed; can become chronic)
common.mechanism: Repetitive patellofemoral joint compression during knee flexion at ground contact under running load; exacerbated by weak hip abductors (hip drop), excessive knee valgus, rearfoot strike pattern, and rapid volume increases.
common.rtpConsiderations: Address hip abductor strength deficits; load management; graduated return to volume; biomechanical retraining if indicated.
common.source: Barton CJ et al. — patellofemoral pain review and management literature

common.name: Tibial bone stress (stress reaction / stress fracture)
common.incidence: moderate — a significant risk in high-mileage middle-distance runners, especially those with low energy availability or high training volume
common.severity: moderate-high (stress fracture = 4–12 weeks+ off impact training; cortical fracture can end season)
common.mechanism: Repetitive bending stress on the tibial cortex from high-volume ground-contact loading exceeding the bone's remodelling capacity; compounded by low energy availability (relative energy deficiency / RED-S), calcium/vitamin D insufficiency, and training surface hardness.
highRiskTissues: tibial shaft (posteromedial — posterior tibial stress syndrome spectrum)

modifiable: biomechanical risk factors (hip drop, increased stride rate)

common.rtpConsiderations: Minimum 4–6 weeks off impact training for stress reaction; 8–12+ weeks for cortical stress fracture; bone health screening (DEXA, nutrition review) before RTP; screen for RED-S.
common.source: Bennell KL et al. — bone stress fracture epidemiology and risk factors; Mountjoy et al. IOC RED-S consensus 2018/2023

common.name: Iliotibial band syndrome (ITBS)
common.incidence: moderate — a common overuse knee complaint at 1500 m-5 km training mileage (high weekly volume plus track interval work)
common.severity: moderate (irritable; usually 2-6 weeks of modified loading, rarely acute time-loss)
common.mechanism: Repetitive loaded knee flexion-extension compressing the distal ITB against the lateral femoral condyle; associated with hip-abductor weakness, increased hip adduction / contralateral pelvic drop, rapid mileage increase and single-direction track running.

modifiable: always running the same track direction

common.rtpConsiderations: Load management + hip-abductor strengthening and mechanics work; graded return once single-leg loading is pain-free. A load + mechanics problem more than a pure strength deficit.
common.source: distance-running overuse epidemiology (van der Worp ITBS systematic review 2012)

injuryProfile.summary: Mixed ACUTE + OVERUSE injury profile. Hamstring strains are acute and velocity-driven (more prevalent at 800/1500 m training paces). Achilles tendinopathy, patellofemoral pain, and tibial bone stress are overuse injuries driven by high training volume and load mismanagement. Tibial bone stress and RED-S (low energy availability) require specific screening in female and weight-conscious athletes. Nordic curls, calf/Achilles loading, and hip abductor strengthening are the primary gym-based prevention levers.

positions.name: 800 m (anaerobic-biased middle distance)
positions.role: The most glycolytically demanding middle-distance event — requires near-sprint speed across two laps with extreme lactate tolerance.
positions.movementDemands: Fast-start acceleration; sustained near-maximal aerobic effort with high glycolytic contribution; decisive sprint finish on the home straight.
positions.runningDemands: Race duration ~1:40–2:10 (elite–club); pace close to 95%+ of VO2max; lactate accumulation is maximal; aerobic power and lactate buffering both decisive.
positions.collisionDemands: none (minor contact in box formation at the start)
positions.speedReq: very high (sub-elite: ~6–7 m/s race pace; elite men: ~7.5 m/s)
positions.powerReq: high (strong finishing kick and tactical surges required)
positions.strengthReq: high (relative strength for economy; power for finishing sprint)
positions.bodyComposition: Lean and powerful relative to build; fast-twitch capacity higher than at longer distances; minimal non-propulsive mass.
gymPriorities: strength for economy (trap-bar DL, squat — heavy, low-rep)
reactive plyometrics for leg stiffness (pogo, bounding)
positions.recoveryConsiderations: High glycolytic and neuromuscular demand per race — 48–72 h recovery after a maximal 800 m effort before quality training. Gym should not be scheduled within 24 h of key interval sessions.

positions.name: 1500 m (mixed aerobic/anaerobic middle distance)
positions.role: The classic middle-distance event — the 'mile' demands a blend of VO2max capacity, lactate threshold, and a decisive finishing kick. The most tactically complex middle-distance event.
positions.movementDemands: Controlled early pace management; sustained aerobic effort at VO2max boundary; one or more tactical surges; all-out sprint in final 200–300 m.
positions.runningDemands: Race duration ~3:30–4:30 (elite–club men); pace at ~95% VO2max sustained; aerobic capacity and lactate threshold are primary physiological determinants; critical speed is highly predictive.
positions.collisionDemands: none (minor tactical contact in pack running)
positions.powerReq: moderate-high (finishing kick and surge capacity essential)
positions.strengthReq: high (relative strength for economy over 3–4 laps)
positions.bodyComposition: Lean; slightly more aerobic profile than 800 m; VO2max-to-weight ratio a key performance determinant.
positions.recoveryConsiderations: High aerobic demand — recovery is aerobic replenishment as much as glycolytic. Gym workload must be managed to avoid compromising interval session quality.

positions.name: 3000–5000 m (aerobic-biased middle/distance)
positions.role: The most aerobically biased middle-distance events — VO2max, critical speed, and running economy dominate performance. The 5 km bridges middle- and long-distance physiology.
positions.movementDemands: Sustained aerobic effort at 90–95% VO2max; economy over 7–12+ minutes; final-lap surge capacity; pacing and glycolytic reserve management.
positions.runningDemands: Race duration ~7:30–14 min (elite–club men); critical speed and running economy are primary performance predictors; lower absolute glycolytic demand than 800/1500 m but finishing kick still decisive.
positions.powerReq: moderate (economy > raw power at this distance)
positions.strengthReq: high (strength for economy at low added mass; calf/Achilles durability for volume)
positions.bodyComposition: Very lean; aerobic efficiency and VO2max-to-weight ratio are key; minimal non-propulsive mass critical.
gymPriorities: strength for economy (heavy, low-rep — not hypertrophy)
tibialis raise (tibial bone stress risk reduction)
low-dose reactive plyometrics (pogo, bounding — dosed against running volume)
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Lower per-session glycolytic cost than 800 m but higher cumulative training volume — gym scheduling must protect the aerobic training week. No heavy lower-body gym within 24 h of key long or threshold runs.

assessments.name: Critical speed / critical velocity (lactate threshold time-trial)
assessments.purpose: Determine the athlete's critical speed — the maximal pace sustainable by aerobic pathways. Predictive of middle-distance race performance and guides training-pace zones. Typically estimated from two or three time-trial efforts at different distances.

targets.elite: event-relative PB tracking; CS as % of VO2max velocity

assessments.source: Jones AM — critical speed and D' literature; Billat interval-training literature

assessments.name: Running economy (submaximal oxygen cost at fixed pace)
assessments.purpose: Measure the oxygen cost (ml/kg/min) of running at a fixed submaximal pace — a primary determinant of middle-distance performance independent of VO2max. Typically measured in a lab at 3–4 speeds; approximated by pace-HR relationship in the field.

targets.elite: track economy improvement vs baseline; elite men ~200 ml/kg/km

assessments.source: Saunders 2004 (factors affecting running economy); Blagrove 2018 (strength training → economy)

assessments.name: Countermovement jump (CMJ) / reactive strength monitoring
assessments.purpose: Monitor neuromuscular freshness (acute readiness) and track reactive strength / leg-stiffness gains from plyometric training. A drop in CMJ flags accumulated neuromuscular fatigue before a key session or race.

targets.elite: within 10% of 4-week baseline for monitoring; track upward trend for stiffness gains

assessments.name: Eccentric hamstring strength (Nordic curl / NordBord)
assessments.purpose: Assess bilateral eccentric hamstring force — a primary modifiable risk factor for hamstring strain, especially relevant at the faster paces of 800 m/1500 m training and race finishes.
equipment: NordBord or equivalent; alternative: Nordic curl load progression
assessments.source: Petersen 2011 Nordic hamstring RCT; van Dyk eccentric-strength testing literature

assessments.name: Calf raise strength / single-leg calf endurance
assessments.purpose: Assess calf and Achilles tendon loading capacity — the primary prehab and return-to-play gate for Achilles tendinopathy. Single-leg calf raise to fatigue or loaded (Silbernagel protocol) is the standard.
assessments.frequency: monthly + on Achilles symptoms + RTP gate

targets.elite: ≥25 single-leg calf raises to fatigue; bilateral symmetry

assessments.source: Silbernagel K — single-leg calf raise as Achilles tendinopathy return-to-sport criterion

assessments.name: Race time (800/1500/3000/5000 m event)
assessments.purpose: The primary outcome measure — race time relative to PB and age-group standards is the defining performance indicator for middle-distance runners.

assessments.name: Hip abductor strength (side-lying hip abduction / single-leg squat drop test)
assessments.purpose: Identify hip abductor weakness linked to hip drop, knee valgus, and elevated patellofemoral and tibial stress injury risk; simple Trendelenburg screen or dynamometer.
equipment: handheld dynamometer (optional); no equipment for screen
assessments.source: Barton CJ; hip-abductor weakness and running-injury literature; expert consensus

assessments.name: Tibial bone stress symptom screen
assessments.purpose: Periodic symptom screen for tibial tenderness, particularly in high-volume training phases and in athletes with low energy availability risk factors; early detection reduces severity of bone-stress injuries.
assessments.frequency: monthly during high-volume phases + on tibial pain

targets.elite: nil tenderness on palpation + nil pain with impact

equipment: palpation / clinical assessment; MRI if indicated
assessments.source: Bennell KL; Mountjoy IOC RED-S consensus 2018/2023; expert consensus

highest: running mechanics (A-skip, arm drive, cadence drills)
lowest: high-volume interval training before aerobic base
heavy loading before growth plates close
youth.trainingEmphasis: Aerobic base first. Running mechanics and coordination habits. Basic bodyweight strength (single-leg squats, hip hinges, core). Protect bone health: adequate nutrition and no sudden volume spikes. No RED-S risk.
commonMistakes: training mileage before aerobic mechanics are established
early high-intensity interval overload
under-fuelling in female youth athletes (RED-S onset)
neglecting strength work entirely

highest: VO2max development (aerobic base + moderate interval work)
lowest: high-load Olympic lifting before power-to-economy transfer need established
non-specific hypertrophy adding mass without economy benefit
development.trainingEmphasis: Build aerobic capacity and running economy simultaneously. Introduce heavy, low-rep strength training. Establish Nordic curl habit. Begin reactive plyometrics conservatively on a strength base. Educate on energy availability.
commonMistakes: skipping strength work in favour of more running volume
plyometric volume before calf/Achilles strength capacity
under-recovery from combined training + strength load
ignoring early Achilles or tibial symptoms

highest: hamstring health (Nordic curl maintenance at fast-pace training periods)
lowest: non-specific gym volume in-season adding fatigue without performance benefit
heavy gym work adjacent to key interval sessions
senior.trainingEmphasis: Individualise strength type (economy-biased heavy strength + reactive plyometrics); protect Achilles and tibiae at high mileage; execute the taper; monitor energy availability.
commonMistakes: adding gym volume in-season without adjusting running load
dropping Nordic curls when programme gets busy
taper mistakes (too much volume retained)
ignoring early Achilles symptoms at volume peaks

lowest: gym exercises that add mass without economy transfer
elite.trainingEmphasis: Data-led economy and critical-speed analysis; individualised strength prescription (evidence of economy response); minimal-effective in-season gym; protect Achilles/tibiae at peak volume; nail the taper.
commonMistakes: too much gym volume at peak running load
ignoring early Achilles load signals
one-size gym programme with insufficient economy data
poor taper management

lowest: aggressive plyometric volume on ageing tendons
masters.trainingEmphasis: Maintain aerobic capacity and running economy conservatively; prioritise Achilles/calf and bone health; increase recovery time between hard sessions; monitor RED-S risk especially in female masters athletes.
commonMistakes: ignoring Achilles / bone-stress early warning signs
under-fuelling (RED-S risk rises in masters)
insufficient recovery between high-load sessions
dropping strength work that protects tendons and bone

offSeason.primaryObjective: Build maximal aerobic base, strength-for-economy foundation, and connective-tissue capacity; address injury risk factors (calf/Achilles, hamstring, tibial bone health).
offSeason.trainingEmphasis: Maximal strength (trap-bar DL, split squat, Nordic curl), calf/Achilles loading, general plyometrics (low intensity), easy-moderate aerobic volume accumulation, mobility work.

programming.source: season-phased S&C: off-season rounds out the physique (Blagrove 2018 strength-for-economy base); in-season narrows to prehab (Nordic/calf, van Dyk 2019)

preSeason.primaryObjective: Convert strength and aerobic base to race-pace-specific fitness; begin interval training; introduce reactive plyometrics; reduce gym volume as running intensity rises.
preSeason.trainingEmphasis: VO2max intervals, threshold work, tempo runs; power plyometrics (pogos, bounding); reduce gym to 2–3 sessions and shift toward reactive/economy work.

programming.source: season-phased S&C: off-season rounds out the physique (Blagrove 2018 strength-for-economy base); in-season narrows to prehab (Nordic/calf, van Dyk 2019)

competition.primaryObjective: Maintain aerobic fitness and economy; protect Achilles/hamstring; execute race-specific sharpening and taper into key competitions.
competition.trainingEmphasis: Reduced gym volume (2 low-volume, high-quality sessions); maintain Nordic curls and calf loading; reactive plyometric priming; race-specific interval and pace work.

programming.source: season-phased S&C: off-season rounds out the physique (Blagrove 2018 strength-for-economy base); in-season narrows to prehab (Nordic/calf, van Dyk 2019)

playoffs.primaryObjective: Peak for target championship — manage heats / semis / finals over multiple days; freshness above all.
playoffs.trainingEmphasis: Minimal-volume priming; recovery between rounds; no development or novel loading.
testingRecommendations: readiness monitoring only — no fatiguing tests

recovery.primaryObjective: Full physical and psychological recovery; address any carried injuries (Achilles, tibial, hamstring); bone health review if needed.
recovery.trainingEmphasis: Low-intensity activity, mobility, light cross-training; maintain calf/Achilles loading if injury-free; medical review of carried issues.
testingRecommendations: bone health / RED-S screen if indicated; injury review; no performance tests

oneMatchPerWeek.pattern: Built around 1–2 quality run sessions (interval/threshold); gym placed to NOT fatigue Achilles/hamstring before key running quality sessions.
oneMatchPerWeek.heavyDay: early-week (Monday/Tuesday), away from key interval or race-pace session
oneMatchPerWeek.powerDay: mid-week small reactive session (pogo, bounding) after or on a moderate running day
oneMatchPerWeek.recoveryDay: day after key interval session or race; pre-race day is light technical/activation only
oneMatchPerWeek.injuryPreventionDay: Nordic curls + single-leg calf + tibialis raise embedded 2×/week; Copenhagen adduction 1–2×/week
oneMatchPerWeek.typicalLoadingPattern: Heavy gym early-week → quality interval session mid-week → easy/recovery → race → recovery.
preferExplosiveWorkDays: dedicated gym day away from key running

twoMatchesPerWeek.pattern: Championship round scheduling (heats + finals): recovery-first between races; no heavy gym during race days.
twoMatchesPerWeek.powerDay: brief priming activation before races if used (drills, jumps, skips)
twoMatchesPerWeek.recoveryDay: between heats/finals and after each race day
twoMatchesPerWeek.injuryPreventionDay: minimal calf and Nordic maintenance only
twoMatchesPerWeek.typicalLoadingPattern: Warm-up → heat → recovery → final. Gym is priming or none.

tournamentOrCongested.pattern: Multi-day championships with multiple rounds; pure freshness and Achilles/injury management.
tournamentOrCongested.injuryPreventionDay: minimal-dose only (calf, drills — no fatigue-inducing work)
tournamentOrCongested.typicalLoadingPattern: Protect recovery and running-mechanics quality between rounds; no development loading.
preferExplosiveWorkDays: race-morning primers only (skips, drills, brief pogo — no fatigue)

transfersWell: heavy trap-bar deadlift / back squat (maximal strength → running economy; 3–6 rep ranges to avoid hypertrophy)
split squat / Bulgarian split squat (single-leg strength, hip-extension robustness, unilateral balance)
Nordic hamstring curl / RDL (hamstring eccentric strength — injury prevention at fast-pace sessions and finishes)
single-leg calf raise (Achilles/calf loading capacity — the most critical tendon prehab for running volume)
tibialis raise (tibial shock absorption — tibial bone-stress risk reduction)
double-leg and single-leg pogo (Achilles tendon stiffness + SSC efficiency — economy and speed-endurance)
bounding / A-skip (running-specific horizontal power and mechanics coordination)
Copenhagen adduction (adductor and groin robustness — hip stability per stride)
Pallof press + dead bug (core anti-rotation/anti-extension — efficient force transfer over thousands of strides)
limitedValue: non-specific hypertrophy (adds non-propulsive mass without economy benefit — counterproductive at all distances)
maximal Olympic lifting volume (some transfer at 800 m; generally optional for middle vs sprint)
heavy eccentric posterior-chain work within 48 h of key interval sessions (pre-fatigues hamstring/Achilles)
high-impact plyometric volume on top of a full running week (cumulative Achilles/tendon overload)
long steady-state low-intensity cardio as gym substitute (no economy or strength transfer)
essentialMovementPatterns: hip hinge (RDL, trap-bar DL — hamstring + posterior chain)
bilateral squat/triple extension (back squat, split squat)
single-leg calf / ankle plantar-flexion (SL calf, pogo)
single-leg hip hinge (SL hinge — unilateral posterior chain)
accessoryPriorities: single-leg calf / Achilles loading (priority #1 for overuse prevention)
Nordic curl / eccentric hamstring (priority #2 — especially at 800/1500 m paces)
hip abductor stability (Copenhagen, lateral band walk)
gymPhilosophy.singleLegEmphasis: High — running is a unilateral cyclic task; single-leg calf, split squat, SL hinge, and step-up build the hip and lower-leg robustness needed to sustain running volume without overuse injury.
gymPhilosophy.olympicLiftingSuitability: Optional — power/hang clean may provide some RFD benefit particularly for 800 m athletes where the finishing sprint is decisive, but is not essential for middle-distance; economy-focused heavy strength + reactive plyometrics deliver more return per training unit.
gymPhilosophy.plyometricEmphasis: Moderate — reactive stiffness training (pogo, bounding, A-skip) builds Achilles tendon stiffness and running economy but must be dosed carefully against already high running volume; avoid large plyometric sessions on the same day as key interval runs.
gymPhilosophy.coreTrainingPhilosophy: Anti-extension and anti-rotation dominate — the trunk and pelvis must maintain position and transfer force efficiently across thousands of strides. Dead bug, Pallof press, hollow hold. Minimal loaded spinal-flexion volume.
gymPhilosophy.rotationalTraining: Low — arm-drive coordination is trained via running mechanics drills; minimal need for dedicated rotational loading.
gymPhilosophy.isometricTraining: Useful in-season and for Achilles/patellar tendinopathy management — isometric calf holds, Spanish squat (patellar tendon), wall-assisted Nordic holds provide tendon stimulus at low fatigue cost.
gymPhilosophy.tempoRecommendations: Controlled heavy tempo on strength work (no grinding fatigue near key sessions); explosive intent on reactive/pogo work; high-rep controlled calf raises for Achilles loading (Silbernagel protocol).
gymPhilosophy.velocityRecommendations: Heavy and slow in off-season (strength-for-economy base); moderate load + explosive intent in pre-season (RFD conversion); minimal-volume, maintained quality in-season. Economy-focused — never chase hypertrophy.

exercises.name: Nordic hamstring curl
exercises.primaryAdaptation: eccentric hamstring strength (biceps femoris) — primary hamstring-strain prevention exercise at fast running paces
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: posterior chain strength and hamstring hypertrophy

exercises.name: Romanian deadlift (RDL)
exercises.movementPattern: hip hinge — eccentric hamstring under load
exercises.primaryAdaptation: hamstring and glute strength at long muscle length — economy and injury prevention

exercises.name: Trap-bar deadlift
exercises.movementPattern: bilateral hip hinge / triple extension — maximal force production
exercises.primaryAdaptation: maximal lower-body strength → running economy (neuromuscular efficiency, force per stride)
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: posterior chain and quad strength; minimal mass gain vs barbell squat

exercises.name: Split squat / Bulgarian split squat
exercises.primaryAdaptation: single-leg strength for economy, hip and knee stability, unilateral load tolerance
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: hip-flexor mobility (rear leg); quad and glute balance

exercises.name: Double-leg pogo jump
exercises.primaryAdaptation: Achilles tendon stiffness + ankle plantar-flexion power — running economy and ground-contact efficiency

exercises.name: Single-leg pogo jump
exercises.primaryAdaptation: single-leg Achilles tendon stiffness and reactive strength — mirrors ground contact in running

exercises.name: Bounding / A-skip
exercises.movementPattern: sprint-specific cyclic horizontal power (horizontal bounding, high knee cycling)
exercises.primaryAdaptation: running-mechanics coordination + horizontal reactive power — economy drills
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: hip-flexor activation in running-specific pattern; Achilles/calf SSC

exercises.name: Single-leg calf raise (loaded)
exercises.movementPattern: ankle plantar-flexion — Achilles tendon and calf loading
exercises.primaryAdaptation: Achilles tendon load capacity + calf strength — primary tendinopathy prevention and RTP exercise

exercises.name: Tibialis raise
exercises.primaryAdaptation: tibialis anterior strength and tibial shock absorption — tibial bone-stress risk reduction
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: shin splints / medial tibial stress syndrome prevention
progressions: loaded tibialis raise (weight plate on foot)

exercises.name: Copenhagen adduction
exercises.movementPattern: hip adduction — adductor and groin loading
exercises.primaryAdaptation: adductor strength and groin robustness — hip stability per running stride

exercises.name: Pallof press (anti-rotation core)
exercises.primaryAdaptation: trunk anti-rotation — force-transfer efficiency across thousands of running strides
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: lumbar stability; pelvic control in the frontal plane

exercises.name: Dead bug (anti-extension core)
exercises.primaryAdaptation: core anti-extension — maintains running posture and force-transfer efficiency over thousands of strides
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: low-back protection under high-volume ground-contact loading

riskFactors: rapid training volume or pace increase
warningSigns: Achilles morning stiffness >10 min post warm-up
tenderness on palpation at mid-substance or insertional Achilles
pain or stiffness after running that worsens over days
single-leg calf raise load capacity drop vs baseline
injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: Single-leg calf raise loaded 2–3×/week year-round; pogo 2×/week in pre-season and in-season; address dorsiflexion mobility daily
exercisesToAvoid: sudden high-volume plyometrics without calf strength base
depth jumps early in the season on unconditioned Achilles
monitoringRecommendations: Achilles soreness NRS before and after sessions
track volume spikes in training load log
injuryPreventionLibrary.source: Alfredson H, Silbernagel K — Achilles tendinopathy eccentric and heavy slow resistance literature

riskFactors: hip drop / knee valgus gait pattern
warningSigns: localised tibial tenderness on palpation (posteromedial / anterior tibia)
tibial pain during or after running that worsens progressively
pain at rest or at night (concerning for cortical stress fracture)
injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: Tibialis raise 2×/week; progress calf loading progressively; screen energy availability in high-risk athletes
exercisesToAvoid: high-volume plyometrics in athletes with active tibial symptoms
monitoringRecommendations: tibial tenderness palpation screen monthly at high mileage
energy availability / RED-S screen in female and weight-conscious athletes
DEXA bone density if repeated bone-stress history
injuryPreventionLibrary.source: Bennell KL — bone stress fracture epidemiology; Mountjoy et al. IOC RED-S consensus 2018/2023

riskFactors: fatigue late in interval sets or finish sprints
warningSigns: proximal posterior thigh tightness or soreness after fast running
reduced NordBord / Nordic curl force output vs baseline
subjective hamstring tightness on high-knee drills or A-skips
injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: Nordic curl 2×/week year-round; RDL 2×/week; single-leg hinge 1–2×/week
exercisesToAvoid: heavy RDL or Nordic within 48 h of key interval session
novel high-load eccentric without progressive introduction
monitoringRecommendations: monthly NordBord bilateral force + L/R ratio
weekly hamstring soreness check before speed or interval sessions
track speed-session volume spikes in training log
injuryPreventionLibrary.source: Petersen 2011 Nordic hamstring RCT; Askling; van Dyk

decisionRules.if: readiness score low (poor sleep + high soreness + low wellness) on any training day
decisionRules.then: autoregulate down one step: replace high-intensity interval or heavy gym session with a technical/easy aerobic session or active recovery; do not attempt maximal intervals or maximal strength when poorly recovered

decisionRules.if: athlete reports systemic illness (fever, below-neck symptoms, infectious illness)
decisionRules.then: withhold all training until symptom-free; resume gradually — no intervals or heavy strength for 48 h after symptom resolution

decisionRules.if: weekly running load (km or session RPE) ACWR > 1.5 vs 28-day chronic baseline
decisionRules.then: cap running volume this week; do not add gym volume; prioritise recovery; flag for coach review
decisionRules.source: Gabbett 2016 (methodology contested — Impellizzeri 2020, Lolli 2019); applied as a soft monitoring input

decisionRules.if: in taper phase (1–2 weeks before target competition)
decisionRules.then: reduce total volume substantially (~40–60%) while MAINTAINING intensity; keep low-volume reactive plyometric and strength priming; maximise recovery; no novel or high-soreness exercises

decisionRules.if: race day or within 24 hours of competition
decisionRules.then: gym/track work is CNS/neuromuscular priming only (a few skips, short strides, brief pogo) or none; no strength development; complete warm-up only

decisionRules.if: athlete reports Achilles soreness or stiffness >10 min after warm-up, OR single-leg calf raise capacity drops vs baseline, OR VISA-A score declining
decisionRules.then: remove high-impact plyometrics (pogos, bounding, single-leg jumps) and reduce calf loading volume; switch to isometric calf holds; flag for physiotherapy review; do not increase running pace until symptom-free
decisionRules.source: Alfredson; Silbernagel — Achilles tendinopathy load-management consensus

decisionRules.then: hold strength gym work at minimal effective volume (2 low-volume high-quality sessions per week); maintain Nordic curl and calf loading; maintain low-volume reactive plyometrics; avoid high-DOMS exercises within 48 h of key running sessions

decisionRules.if: a key interval, threshold, or race-pace running session is scheduled within 24 hours
decisionRules.then: avoid heavy lower-body gym (squats, trap-bar DL, RDL, Nordic curl, depth jumps) the day before — preserve legs and Achilles/calf freshness for running quality; light upper-body or core session is permissible
decisionRules.source: expert consensus (running-session priority sequencing); residual-fatigue and running-economy literature

acwr.model: Acute (7-day) : chronic (28-day) of running volume load (km or session RPE); rolling EWMA preferred to reduce day-to-day variability
acwr.source: Gabbett 2016 — methodology contested (Impellizzeri 2020, Lolli 2019); used as a soft monitoring input only

loadManagement.weeklyProgressionGuideline: Avoid >~10% week-to-week spike in total running volume or intensity; the Achilles tendon, tibiae, and hamstrings are the primary risk tissues under volume spikes.

gymVolumeRanges.offSeason: high (3 sessions; strength-for-economy + plyometric base + prehab foundation)
gymVolumeRanges.inSeason: low-moderate maintenance (2 sessions; minimal effective volume, maintained quality, no DOMS near key runs)

loadManagement.minimumEffectiveVolume: ~2 low-volume gym sessions/week sustain economy-related strength in-season; single-leg calf and Nordic curl must NOT drop to zero year-round.
loadManagement.maximumAdaptiveVolume: Off-season — build maximal strength and Achilles/calf loading capacity when distance from competition allows full recovery between sessions.
loadManagement.maximumRecoverableVolume: Constrained by total running volume (the dominant recovery demand); gym must never compromise the quality of aerobic or interval running sessions.
loadManagement.deloadRecommendations: Planned deload every 3–4 weeks in development phases; auto-deload on Achilles soreness, hamstring tightness, CMJ drop, or ACWR >1.5. Competition taper is a planned performance deload.
loadManagement.progressionRules: Progress gym load when quality met at target RPE and tendons are symptom-free; prefer intensity over volume in-season; progress plyometric complexity only after calf/Achilles strength base is established.
loadManagement.regressionRules: On Achilles or tibial soreness, drop running volume and plyometric load first; reduce calf/posterior-chain gym load; never schedule heavy lower-body gym within 24 h of key running.
loadManagement.missedSessionRules: Do not stack missed interval sessions; resume at planned level. After time off (esp. Achilles/bone-stress injury), rebuild running volume gradually (≤10%/week) with symptom and load monitoring.
loadManagement.source: Mujika/Bosquet (taper); Gabbett (load — contested); Rønnestad/Blagrove (maintenance + economy); Alfredson/Silbernagel (Achilles); Bennell (bone stress); Saw 2016

factors.name: Achilles / calf soreness (sport-specific)

thresholds.when: Achilles morning stiffness >10 min post warm-up or VISA-A declining
thresholds.modifier: remove high-impact plyometrics and high-pace running; calf isometrics only; flag for physio

factors.source: Alfredson; Silbernagel; Achilles tendinopathy load-management consensus

thresholds.modifier: convert to recovery / easy aerobic session

thresholds.when: high prior session load + short recovery (<36 h) before key interval
thresholds.modifier: lower today's running or gym intensity
reduce high-intensity intervals and gym volume; treat as accumulated fatigue

thresholds.when: sustained suppression vs baseline trend over 3+ days
thresholds.modifier: treat as accumulating fatigue; ease interval load and gym intensity
possible fatigue or illness — caution before high-intensity sessions
reduce load; maintain prehab and calf loading
recovery-first; gym is priming or none
reduce intensity; prioritise sleep and recovery

readinessModel.notes: Achilles/calf soreness is elevated to a top-priority, sport-specific readiness input — it should GATE all reactive plyometric and high-pace running. Subjective wellness, sleep, and prior session load carry the most general weight. HRV is a moderate additional signal when trended over multiple days. Raw vitals (HRV/RHR/sleep) stay private to the athlete; the coach sees only the derived readiness score.

coachDashboard.principle: Coach sees DERIVED signals and availability only — never an individual athlete's raw HRV, sleep, or resting HR. Aggregated, plain-English, action-oriented.
mostUsefulKpis: training availability (fit/modified/out — especially Achilles and tibial)
weekly km vs plan (per athlete/event group)
mostUsefulAlerts: Achilles soreness flag on any athlete
weeklyReports: running volume vs plan (per athlete/event group)
coachDashboard.trafficLightIndicators: Per-athlete green/amber/red from the derived readiness + load state (no raw numbers shown).
coachDashboard.privacyNote: All per-athlete entries here are DERIVED (readiness score, load_state, ACWR, adherence %, injury availability). Raw vitals are excluded by design and enforced by the schema validator.

strongEvidence: heavy strength training improves running economy in middle- and long-distance runners (Blagrove 2018 systematic review; L2)
single-leg calf raise loading is the primary evidence-based Achilles tendinopathy intervention (Alfredson; Silbernagel)
subjective wellness is a sensitive readiness indicator (Saw 2016)
taper improves middle-distance performance — reduce volume, maintain intensity (Mujika/Padilla; Bosquet 2007)
Nordic hamstring protocol reduces hamstring strain incidence (Petersen 2011 RCT; L1)
critical speed is a robust predictor of middle-distance performance (Jones; Billat)
weakEvidence: exact ACWR thresholds for running injury risk (contested methodology)
optimal ratio of strength:plyometric:running volume for economy in middle-distance
whether Olympic lifting provides incremental benefit over heavy strength + plyometrics for middle distance
specific gym volume thresholds for peak middle-distance performance
areasRequiringExpertJudgement: balance between running volume (aerobic capacity) and gym load (economy/stiffness) — both compete for recovery
individual response to strength training on running economy (some non-responders exist)
Achilles load management during high-mileage pre-season without losing running volume
RED-S / energy availability assessment and nutrition referral in female athletes
areasRequiringFutureResearch: optimal Nordic curl + calf loading programme integrated within a full middle-distance training week
AI/wearable real-time economy and stiffness feedback
personalised running-economy response to strength training
bone health and RED-S prevention protocols in masters middle-distance runners
potentialRisksIfMisimplemented: heavy gym work adjacent to key interval sessions (impairs running quality and Achilles recovery)
dropping calf/Nordic prehab when programme busy (removes the primary tendinopathy/hamstring prevention lever)
treating ACWR as a hard rule rather than a soft signal
exposing raw vitals to coaches (privacy + trust breach)
botched taper — too much volume retained, performance suppressed
non-screening for RED-S / low energy availability in at-risk athletes

kpis.name: Readiness
kpis.measurementMethod: Composite of subjective wellness + sleep + prior load + Achilles/calf soreness (+ optional CMJ and HRV trend), normalised to baseline
kpis.source: Saw 2016; derived score (raw vitals stay private)

kpis.name: Critical speed
kpis.measurementMethod: Critical speed estimated from two or three time-trial efforts at different distances (e.g. 1200 m and 2400 m) using the linear distance-time model
kpis.source: Jones AM — critical speed literature; Billat

kpis.name: Running economy
kpis.measurementMethod: Oxygen cost of running at a fixed submaximal pace (lab); or pace-HR ratio at a fixed effort level (field proxy via wearable)
kpis.targetRange: improving trend; lower ml/kg/km or lower HR at fixed pace
kpis.eliteBenchmark: elite men ~200 ml/kg/km at race pace
equipmentRequired: metabolic cart (lab) or GPS watch + HR monitor (field proxy)

kpis.name: Weekly consistency
kpis.measurementMethod: % prescribed sessions (running + gym + prehab + check-ins) completed

kpis.name: Training availability
kpis.measurementMethod: fit / modified / out (status only — especially Achilles, tibial, hamstring)

kpis.name: Running volume ACWR
kpis.measurementMethod: 7-day:28-day running volume (km or session RPE load)

kpis.name: Race time (event performance)
kpis.measurementMethod: Race / time-trial time for athlete's primary event (800/1500/3000/5000 m)

kpis.name: Sleep
kpis.measurementMethod: Wearable / self-report sleep duration and quality

kpis.name: HRV
kpis.measurementMethod: Morning HRV (rMSSD), trended vs rolling baseline
kpis.eliteBenchmark: stable / upward trend (aerobic training typically elevates HRV)

kpis.name: Resting HR
kpis.measurementMethod: Morning resting heart rate vs personal baseline
kpis.source: expert consensus (PRIVATE — athlete-only; rolls into readiness)

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Readiness
athleteDashboardKpis.why: One daily signal telling the middle-distance runner whether to push or hold back — the most actionable single number, anchoring Achilles and overall training quality decisions.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Race time trend
athleteDashboardKpis.why: The outcome every middle-distance runner cares about most — their time, improving vs their own baseline across their event.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Critical speed
athleteDashboardKpis.why: The most powerful leading indicator of middle-distance race performance — tracks aerobic and lactate fitness gains between races.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Running economy
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Makes the invisible gains from strength training visible — a more economical stride means faster racing for the same effort, directly linked to gym work.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Weekly consistency
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Middle-distance adaptation is built on relentless aerobic accumulation — consistency over weeks beats occasional perfect sessions.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Achilles resilience (calf raise capacity)
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Makes the primary tendon injury risk visible and trainable — a calf raise milestone is both a performance and injury-prevention win.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Availability streak
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Celebrates injury-free training weeks — the Achilles-healthy and tibial-healthy streak is the most important career-longevity metric.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Volume ACWR
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Shows whether training load is in the productive zone or spiking toward overuse injury — the primary load-management guardrail.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Squad readiness
coachDashboardKpis.why: At-a-glance freshness (traffic-light, derived) to shape the session before it starts — especially relevant on high-volume training days.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Training availability
coachDashboardKpis.why: Who is fit / modified / out (especially Achilles and tibial) — the critical daily planning input for a running squad.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Achilles / injury risk flags
coachDashboardKpis.why: Surfaces athletes with Achilles soreness or tibial symptoms needing immediate load adjustment or physio referral.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Running volume ACWR distribution
coachDashboardKpis.why: Flags load-spike risk athletes proactively for volume management before injury onset.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Weekly km vs plan (per athlete/event group)
coachDashboardKpis.why: Shows who is over- or under-loaded relative to planned training volume.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Training completion / compliance
coachDashboardKpis.why: Whether prescribed interval sessions and prehab (calf loading, Nordic curls) are actually completed.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Meet readiness (taper state)
coachDashboardKpis.why: Taper / freshness picture into a key competition — shaping race-week decisions for each athlete.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Critical speed trend (event group)
coachDashboardKpis.why: Derived performance signal showing whether the group's fitness is on track without exposing raw vitals.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Recovery trend (squad)
coachDashboardKpis.why: Derived readiness trend warns of accumulating fatigue across a training block before it shows up as injury.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Injury / illness status summary
coachDashboardKpis.why: Availability picture (status only) for planning + medical liaison.

coachDashboardKpis.name: CMJ drop flags
coachDashboardKpis.why: Identifies athletes carrying accumulated neuromuscular fatigue before a key interval session or race.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Fatigue distribution
coachDashboardKpis.why: Spread of green / amber / red shows whether the whole squad or just individuals need load adjustment.

performanceScore.philosophy: Reflects progress toward the aerobic, economic, and lactate-tolerance demands of competitive middle-distance running, weighted to reward the qualities that determine race outcomes (economy, critical speed, availability) while penalising injury risk, Achilles fragility, and excessive fatigue — never rewarding training through pain.

components.rationale: Aerobic adaptation is built on consistent training accumulation — the single most controllable performance lever.
Achilles-healthy, tibial-healthy availability is the strongest performance lever — injured athletes don't adapt.
Race-time improvement is the primary performance outcome for every middle-distance athlete.
Critical speed tracks the primary aerobic performance determinant between races.
Economy improvement is the mechanism by which strength training converts to race performance — a leading indicator.
Penalises chronic fatigue and poor recovery; keeps the score sustainable across a long season.
Mild penalty for load-spiking patterns that increase overuse injury risk.

guardrails: never increases for training through Achilles pain, tibial tenderness, red readiness, or injury
consistency + availability dominate so the score cannot be gamed by occasional maximal race-day efforts
CMJ drop or poor readiness caps the score when neuromuscular fatigue is high
performanceScore.explainability: Each component is shown with its contribution so the athlete sees exactly why the score moved and what to work on next — economy gains from the gym are made visible.

gamification.name: Achilles-healthy weeks
gamification.rewards: Consecutive weeks training and racing without Achilles soreness — tied to the sport's primary overuse injury risk.

gamification.name: Calf raise load milestone
gamification.rewards: Personal bests in loaded single-leg calf raise — links injury prevention directly to a concrete, achievable gym target.

gamification.name: Consistency streak
gamification.rewards: Unbroken weeks hitting prescribed running + gym sessions; rewards process over outcome.

gamification.name: Critical speed PB
gamification.rewards: Improvement in estimated critical speed — the most meaningful between-race fitness marker for middle-distance athletes.

gamification.name: Economy milestone
gamification.rewards: Improvement in running economy (pace-HR proxy trend) — makes gym-to-race transfer tangible and rewarding.

gamification.name: Personal-best milestones
gamification.rewards: Race-time PBs vs the athlete's own baseline — self-referenced, never leaderboard.

gamification.name: Testing-battery completion
gamification.rewards: Completing each testing block (critical speed time-trials, calf raise, CMJ) — encourages objective tracking.
